PERSONNEL AND PAYROLL RECORD RETENTION DURATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

POLICY DECLARATION AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this Personnel and Payroll Record Retention Duration Information Sheet to describe, as a matter of California and federal law, how long Acme, Inc. is required to keep the personnel records and payroll records it maintains relating to Jordan Lee and other employees, and where those records must be kept. This information sheet is about the employer's underlying duty to retain records for a set period — it does not describe, and should not be confused with, the separate statutory right of a current or former employee to inspect or receive a copy of those records, which is addressed in this project's separate Employee's Request to Inspect Personnel and Payroll Records document. This is a statement of general legal requirements; it does not state what Acme, Inc. should do about any particular record, and it is not a substitute for Acme, Inc.'s own document-retention schedule or legal advice.

PERSONNEL RECORDS: AT LEAST THREE YEARS AFTER TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, UNDER § 1198.5(C)(1)
Separately from the inspection right described elsewhere in this project's documents, Labor Code § 1198.5(c) imposes an affirmative duty on Acme, Inc. to keep personnel records for a minimum period, regardless of whether any employee ever asks to inspect them. With regard to all employees, § 1198.5(c)(1) requires Acme, Inc. to maintain a copy of each employee's personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment. The statute's trigger for this duration is termination of employment, not the date a given record was created — so a personnel record created early in a long employment relationship must still be kept for at least three years measured from when that employment relationship ends, not three years from when the record itself was made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "With regard to all employees, maintain a copy of each employee’s personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel-records retention duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim about how long any particular document should actually be kept in a specific case (a longer period may be prudent, or required by some other law not addressed here). This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 1198.5(c)(1); no additional independent source was sought for this specific duration figure. This clause does not restate § 1198.5(c)(2)-(3), the same subdivision's separate rules on where and how a current or former employee's records must be made available once a request is made — those rules govern the inspection process, addressed in this project's separate personnel-records-request document, not the retention duration itself.

PAYROLL RECORDS: AT LEAST THREE YEARS ON FILE, AT THE WORKPLACE OR A CENTRAL CALIFORNIA LOCATION, UNDER § 226(A)
Labor Code § 226(a) requires Acme, Inc. to furnish an itemized wage statement to Jordan Lee and other employees with each payment of wages, and it separately requires Acme, Inc. to keep records of the deductions made. The deductions made from payment of wages must be recorded in ink or other indelible form, properly dated, showing the month, day, and year, and a copy of the wage statement together with the record of the deductions must be kept on file by Acme, Inc. for at least three years, at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California. Unlike the personnel-records duration described elsewhere in this document, § 226(a) does not state termination of employment as the event that starts this three-year period running; by its terms, the requirement is that the copy and deduction record be "kept on file" for at least three years, without conditioning that duration on when (or whether) the employment relationship ends.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a copy of the statement and the record of the deductions shall be kept on file by the employer for at least three years at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's payroll-records retention duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 226(a); no additional independent source was sought for this specific duration and location figure. This same statutory language is also the subject of this project's separate Wage Statement Itemization Policy document, which addresses the nine required content items of an itemized wage statement in full; this clause addresses only the retention-duration and location requirement within that same subdivision, not the content requirements themselves. This clause does not resolve, for a specific record created mid-employment, exactly which date within the employment relationship the three-year period is measured from (for example, the date of the pay period, the date the statement was furnished, or some other date) — the statutory text quoted here states only that the copy and deduction record must be kept on file for the stated minimum duration, without further specifying the precise starting date for that calculation.

TWO DIFFERENT THREE-YEAR PERIODS, NOT ONE: COMPARING THE § 1198.5(C)(1) AND § 226(A) RETENTION DURATIONS
It is easy to assume that because both the personnel-records retention duty and the payroll-records retention duty are commonly described as "three years," they describe the same three-year period. They do not. Labor Code § 1198.5(c)(1) requires Acme, Inc. to maintain a copy of each employee's personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment — a duration expressly triggered by the end of the employment relationship. Labor Code § 226(a), by contrast, requires that a copy of the wage statement and the record of deductions be kept on file by the employer for at least three years at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California — language that states a minimum period the records must remain on file, without tying the start of that period to termination of employment at all. Because the two statutes name different triggers, a payroll record and a personnel record created on the same day, for the same still-employed worker, are not necessarily required to be destroyed or retained on the same schedule: the payroll-records duty under § 226(a) is, by its terms, already running while the employee remains employed, while the personnel-records duty under § 1198.5(c)(1) does not even begin to run until that employment ends. The two statutes also differ in a second respect: § 226(a) specifies where the payroll records must be kept (the place of employment or a central location within California), while the text of § 1198.5(c)(1) quoted here states no comparable location requirement for personnel records.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "With regard to all employees, maintain a copy of each employee’s personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  "a copy of the statement and the record of the deductions shall be kept on file by the employer for at least three years at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is one state's two statutes, used as real evidence that California's personnel-records and payroll-records retention durations are textually distinct rather than a single unified rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The two citations below are to two different California statutes (Labor Code §§ 1198.5(c)(1) and 226(a)), not two subsections of the same statute, so no same-section duplication is being treated as two independent sources; the same two subdivisions are also each cited and quoted independently, for their own separate points, in the two clauses of this document that precede this one. This clause does not address whether some other law not examined here (for example, a wage order, an industry-specific regulation, or a different Labor Code section) might impose a longer retention period for either category of record in a specific case; it compares only the text of these two statutes.

A THIRD, FEDERALLY DISTINCT DURATION FOR FORM I-9: THE LATER OF THREE YEARS AFTER HIRE OR ONE YEAR AFTER TERMINATION
Form I-9 sits outside the two California retention durations described in this document, because it is governed by a separate federal statute rather than by Labor Code §§ 1198.5 or 226. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(3), after completion of Form I-9, Acme, Inc. must retain a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form and make it available for inspection by specified federal officials, during a period beginning on the date of hiring and, in the case of the hiring of an individual, ending three years after the date of such hiring, or one year after the date the individual's employment is terminated, whichever is later. This is a third, distinct duration formula: unlike the flat three-years-after-termination period for personnel records under § 1198.5(c)(1), and unlike the flat at-least-three-years-on-file period for payroll records under § 226(a), the I-9 duration under § 1324a(b)(3) is the later of two alternative measurements, one running from hire and one running from termination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "After completion of such form in accordance with paragraphs (1) and (2), the person or entity must retain a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form and make it available for inspection by officers of the Service, the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, or the Department of Labor during a period beginning on the date of the hiring, recruiting, or referral of the individual and ending— (A) in the case of the recruiting or referral for a fee (without hiring) of an individual, three years after the date of the recruiting or referral, and (B) in the case of the hiring of an individual— (i) three years after the date of such hiring, or (ii) one year after the date the individual’s employment is terminated, whichever is later."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, retention of verification form (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324a)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a third retention-duration formula for a specific document (Form I-9) that is distinct from the two California retention durations otherwise addressed in this information sheet — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation. This project's separate I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification Information Sheet already addresses this same statutory retention rule in more depth (including the officials named in the statute who may inspect the retained form); this clause states it briefly for comparison purposes only, and was independently re-verified against the same primary source (Cornell Legal Information Institute's text of 8 U.S.C. § 1324a) in this session rather than copied without a fresh check. This clause does not address whether some other federal or state law imposes a different retention period for any other specific hiring-related document; it addresses only the Form I-9 duration under § 1324a(b)(3).

WHAT THE STATUTES ACTUALLY SAY ABOUT FAILING TO RETAIN, AS OPPOSED TO FAILING TO PERMIT INSPECTION
The two statutes described in this document treat the consequence of a retention failure differently, and neither one states a penalty that is worded as applying specifically and only to a failure to retain. Labor Code § 1198.5(k) states a $750 penalty, recoverable by the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner, where an employer "fails to permit a current or former employee, or their representative, to inspect or copy personnel records within the times specified in this section" — a penalty keyed to a failure to permit timely inspection or copying once a request is made, not to a failure to retain records for the three-year period standing alone. If Acme, Inc. did not retain a given personnel record for the required period and, as a result, could not produce it in response to a timely request, that would likely trigger the § 1198.5(k) inspection-failure penalty in practice — but the statutory text of § 1198.5(k) itself is written around the failure to permit inspection, not around the retention duty in § 1198.5(c)(1) directly. Labor Code § 226 is structured differently: the retention-duration sentence itself is written into the same subdivision, § 226(a), that also states the wage-statement content requirements, and § 226(e)(1) provides that an employee suffering injury as a result of a knowing and intentional failure by an employer to comply with subdivision (a) is entitled to recover the greater of all actual damages or fifty dollars ($50) for the initial pay period in which a violation occurs and one hundred dollars ($100) per employee for each violation in a subsequent pay period, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of four thousand dollars ($4,000), and is entitled to an award of costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Because the retention sentence sits inside subdivision (a) itself, a failure to comply with that retention sentence falls within the literal scope of what § 226(e)(1) calls "a failure by an employer to comply with subdivision (a)" — though § 226(e)(1) also requires that the failure be knowing and intentional and that the employee suffer injury as a result, elements this document does not resolve for any specific case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If an employer fails to permit a current or former employee, or their representative, to inspect or copy personnel records within the times specified in this section, or times agreed to by mutual agreement as provided in this section, the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner may recover a penalty of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) from the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(k) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1198.5.)
  "An employee suffering injury as a result of a knowing and intentional failure by an employer to comply with subdivision (a) is entitled to recover the greater of all actual damages or fifty dollars ($50) for the initial pay period in which a violation occurs and one hundred dollars ($100) per employee for each violation in a subsequent pay period, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of four thousand dollars ($4,000), and is entitled to an award of costs and reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.)
  Known gap: This is two of California's statutes, used as real evidence of what each one's text actually says (and does not say) about a retention failure specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim that a court has actually applied § 226(e)(1)'s penalty to a pure retention failure (as opposed to a wage-statement content defect) in a reported decision; no case law on that specific application was located or relied on here, only the statutory text itself. The § 1198.5(k) citation below is the same subdivision already quoted, independently, in this project's separate personnel-records-request document; it is not a new source, and it is quoted here for the different, narrower point that its penalty is worded around inspection failure rather than retention failure as such. The § 226(e)(1) citation is a different subdivision of § 226 than the § 226(a) retention text quoted elsewhere in this document, so the two are not the same textual passage, though they are subsections of the same statutory section and are not being counted as independent sources from one another. This clause does not identify any additional, free-standing statutory penalty — beyond the two described here — that applies specifically to a bare failure to retain personnel or payroll records where no inspection request was ever made and no wage-statement defect occurred; if such a penalty exists elsewhere in California law, it was not located in this session's research and is not asserted here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURE
Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed a copy of this Personnel and Payroll Record Retention Duration Information Sheet. Jordan Lee understands that it describes Acme, Inc.'s statutory retention obligations for personnel and payroll records under California law, and, for Form I-9 specifically, under federal law — and that it does not describe how long Acme, Inc. in fact keeps any particular record, which may exceed these statutory minimums. Questions about Acme, Inc.'s actual record-retention practices, or about how to exercise the separate right to inspect or copy a specific personnel or payroll record, may be directed to Acme, Inc. using the process described in this project's separate Employee's Request to Inspect Personnel and Payroll Records document.
